source: WETH9 canonical implementation + Solidity docs — balance accounting
mechanism: A token contract keeps an internal balanceOf ledger per user while totalSupply() reads address(this).balance (or a separate supply var). Any path that transfers ETH into the contract without crediting balanceOf (donation, forced send, selfdestruct) or any path that credits balanceOf without an offsetting ledger update desynchronizes the two ledgers.
root_cause: Two independent accounting sources (per-user balanceOf vs aggregate supply/balance) that are not updated by the same code paths; value can enter or leave one ledger without the other.
preconditions: an internal per-user balance mapping exists alongside an aggregate balance/supply read
a function credits/debits one ledger without the matching ledger update
value can reach the contract address without minting (forced send, receive, selfdestruct) or an offsetting transfer is skipped on some exit path
exploit_sequence: attacker identifies an exit path that transfers ETH without zeroing/decrementing the per-user ledger (or an entry path that credits the ledger without the ETH arriving)
repeat the asymmetric path to inflate the withdrawable ledger above the real balance
drain the contract against the inflated ledger
impact: Users can withdraw more than the contract actually holds (insolvency) or funds are stuck unreachable by any balanceOf holder.
remediation: Keep ONE accounting source of truth: totalSupply() should sum balanceOf (or a tracked supply var updated in lockstep with every transfer/deposit/withdraw); never read raw address balance for liability accounting.
code_evidence:
function withdraw(uint wad) public { require(balanceOf[msg.sender] >= wad); balanceOf[msg.sender] -= wad; msg.sender.transfer(wad); } // balanced
// BAD: totalSupply() { return this.balance; } while balanceOf tracks deposits separately
corrected_code: function withdraw(uint wad) public { require(balanceOf[msg.sender] >= wad); balanceOf[msg.sender] -= wad; totalSupply -= wad; msg.sender.transfer(wad); }

mechanism: Cross-function accounting bypass: a check performed in one function (e.g. a limit, a flag, a status) is rendered stale by a second function that changes the checked state before the first function's effect is finalized, so a multi-call sequence passes each individual guard but violates the invariant.
root_cause: Guard and effect live in different functions with no atomicity; a caller can interleave calls to reset the precondition or advance the state between check and use.
preconditions: function A checks a condition and stores/uses the result
function B mutates the state A checked, callable between A's check and A's effect
the sequence A -> B -> (repeat) passes every single-call guard
exploit_sequence: call A to pass a limit/flag check (e.g. deposit within cap)
call B to reset/raise the cap or clear the flag
repeat A to exceed the intended bound; each single call is individually 'valid'
withdraw or mint against the inflated allowance
impact: Limits, caps, and state-machine invariants are bypassable by an interleaved call sequence.
remediation: Make the checked state and the effect atomic (same transaction, re-check after every external call, or use a monotonic non-resettable counter); re-read the guard inside the effect.
code_evidence:
function deposit(uint amt) external { require(bal + amt <= cap); bal += amt; } // cap check here
function setCap(uint c) external onlyOwner { cap = c; } // cap changed between calls
corrected_code: function deposit(uint amt) external { require(bal + amt <= cap, 'cap'); bal += amt; } // re-check inside; cap changes do not retroactively allow past deposits

source: public audit corpus — reentrancy guard applied to one path only
mechanism: Cross-function reentrancy: a nonReentrant guard (or CEI ordering) is applied in the primary external function, but a second function shares the same mutable state and lacks the guard — the attacker re-enters the unguarded function from the callback, corrupting state the guarded function assumed was stable.
root_cause: Reentrancy protection is per-function rather than per-shared-state; the guard does not cover every function that reads/writes the same state touched during the external call.
preconditions: function A has an external call and a guard/CEI ordering
function B (unguarded) reads or writes state that A also uses, and is reachable during A's callback
the callback can invoke B before A completes
exploit_sequence: call A, which performs an external call to a callback-capable address
inside the callback, call B (unguarded) which mutates shared state A relies on
A resumes using the corrupted state (e.g. wrong balance, double-credited amount)
repeat to extract value
impact: Draining or state corruption via a second, unguarded function sharing the vulnerable state.
remediation: Guard every function that touches the same state as any external-calling function; prefer guards at the shared-state layer or use CEI ordering consistently across all writers.
code_evidence:
function claim() external nonReentrant { reward = calc(); safeTransfer(msg.sender, reward); state.claimed=true; } // guarded
function donate() external { state.donations += msg.value; } // unguarded writer of shared state
corrected_code:
function claim() external nonReentrant { ... }
function donate() external nonReentrant { state.donations += msg.value; } // same guard family

mechanism: Cross-contract read-only reentrancy: contract X (a consumer/router) calls contract Y (a pool) during an external callback while Y's state is mid-mutation; Y's view function returns temporarily inconsistent values that X acts on, letting the attacker arbitrage/claim against stale state across two contracts.
root_cause: A view/read path in one contract reads state that another contract mutates across an external-call boundary; the reader does not enforce that the state is settled.
preconditions: contract Y performs an external call before finalizing its state
contract X (different contract) reads Y's state during the callback window
X acts on the intermediate value (price, balance, reward)
exploit_sequence: attacker enters Y's vulnerable function, triggering an external callback
during the callback, the attacker calls X which reads Y's unstable state
X acts on the skewed value (swap, mint, claim)
revert/complete and profit from the skew
impact: Cross-contract loss as consumers act on corrupted intermediate state.
remediation: Finalize all state before external calls in Y; make Y's view functions revert or return settled values during reentrancy (guard on view entry points consumed by other contracts).
code_evidence:
// Y: claim() { externalCall(); updateState(); }
// X: function read() view returns(uint) { return Y.getPrice(); } // reads mid-callback
corrected_code: // Y: claim() { updateState(); externalCall(); }  // CEI in Y; X now reads settled state

source: public audit corpus — withdraw-revert griefing / send failure
mechanism: A withdraw path uses send()/transfer() (fixed 2300 gas) to a contract that cannot receive ETH, or ignores the boolean return of a low-level call — the failure either bricks the entire withdrawal for all users sharing the iteration (griefing) or silently skips the transfer while the ledger is debited.
root_cause: Fixed-gas transfer/send to arbitrary recipients, or an unchecked low-level call result, combined with state updates that assume success.
preconditions: withdraw loop iterates over multiple recipients
one recipient reverts on receive (malicious or just a contract needing more gas)
or: low-level call return boolean discarded before the ledger is updated
exploit_sequence: attacker registers a recipient that reverts on ETH receipt
any batch payout that includes the attacker reverts the whole transaction
other users' withdrawals are blocked (DoS) — or the attacker makes a call fail and the ledger is still debited
impact: Funds stuck (griefing/DoS) or silent loss when the call fails but the ledger says otherwise.
remediation: Use pull-payment (each user withdraws individually), check and require() every low-level call result before mutating the ledger, and never rely on fixed 2300-gas send/transfer to arbitrary recipients.
code_evidence:
address payable[] memory payees; for (i...) payees[i].send(payAmt); // fixed gas + unchecked
// or: (bool ok,) = dest.call{value: v}(""); balances[dest] -= v; // debits regardless of ok
corrected_code: require(dest.send(payAmt), 'send failed'); // or pull-payment: claim() pattern with per-user balance

source: first-depositor / share inflation attack (public audit corpus)
mechanism: First-depositor share inflation: when totalSupply == 0, the first depositor mints shares at a 1:1 unit price, then donates assets (direct transfer) to inflate totalAssets. The next depositor's shares = assets * supply / totalAssets round toward zero (or to a tiny number), so the attacker redeems and captures the victim's deposit.
root_cause: Share price is derived from raw balance/totalAssets which donations can inflate, and the first mint sets the exchange rate; no minimum/minted-dead shares.
preconditions: share math: shares = assets * totalSupply / totalAssets
direct transfers (donations) to the vault are possible and count toward totalAssets
first-depositor window (totalSupply == 0)
exploit_sequence: attacker deposits 1 wei (or minimal) to become the price-setter
donates a large asset amount directly to inflate totalAssets
victim deposits; their minted shares round to nearly zero
attacker redeems, taking the victim's deposit
impact: Complete loss of the next depositor's funds.
remediation: Mint dead shares / virtual offset on first deposit, or track assets via an internal accounting variable that only deposits update (never raw balance), or enforce a minimum first deposit that makes inflation uneconomical.
code_evidence: function convertToShares(uint assets) view returns (uint) { return assets * totalSupply / totalAssets; } // raw balance ratio
corrected_code: uint internal _totalAssets; // updated only in deposit/redeem, never via balanceOf(this)

source: Chainlink manipulation/staleness guidance (public oracle audit corpus)
mechanism: Price/feed values are used without validating staleness, deviation bounds, or the returned round; a stale or manipulated feed (or a spot price derived from a thin pool) is accepted as the reference value, enabling under-collateralized borrowing or unfair swap pricing.
root_cause: The oracle return is trusted as-is: no staleness check, no sanity/deviation bound, no manipulation-resistance for spot-derived prices.
preconditions: value-bearing logic reads an oracle price (Chainlink latestRoundData, spot reserves, self-reported)
the price can be stale, out of deviation, or manipulable at low cost
the protocol acts on the price (borrow, swap, collateral, mint)
exploit_sequence: attacker makes the feed stale (waits) or moves a thin spot source with a large swap
or the aggregator returns an out-of-deviation value that is accepted
borrow/swap/mint against the skewed price
unwind at the true price and keep the difference
impact: Under-collateralized loans, bad debt, or direct value extraction.
remediation: Validate latestRoundData: answeredInRound >= roundId, updatedAt within a freshness window, and price within deviation bounds of a second source; never use a single manipulable spot for value-bearing decisions.
code_evidence: ( , int price, , uint updatedAt, ) = feed.latestRoundData(); use(price); // no staleness/deviation check
corrected_code: require(updatedAt >= block.timestamp - MAX_STALE, 'stale'); require(price > 0 && price < MAX_DEVIATION_BOUND, 'bad price');

source: proxy initialization / UUPS takeover (public audit corpus)
mechanism: An upgradeable implementation exposes initialize() without an initializer guard (or the proxy is deployed and left uninitialized), so any caller can invoke initialize() to become owner/admin before the legitimate deployer does, then upgrade or drain.
root_cause: initialize() lacks the initializer/disabling guard; implementation constructor cannot run in delegatecall context, so nothing blocks a re-initialization.
preconditions: logic contract has initialize-style setup
no initializer modifier and no _disableInitializers() in the constructor
proxy deployed without immediate initialization, or an implementation deployed standalone
exploit_sequence: attacker watches for a freshly deployed proxy/implementation
front-runs or simply calls initialize(attacker) before the owner does
attacker sets themselves as owner/admin
upgrade the proxy to a malicious implementation or drain
remediation: Apply the initializer modifier to every initialize(); call _disableInitializers() in implementation constructors; initialize atomically at deployment.
code_evidence: function initialize(address owner_) external { owner = owner_; } // no initializer guard
corrected_code: function initialize(address owner_) external initializer { owner = owner_; }

source: permit / EIP-2612 replay + cross-chain (public audit corpus)
mechanism: A signed permit (EIP-2612) lacks a nonce/domain separation that is unique per chain or per deployment, so a signature captured on one chain (or before a redeploy) is replayed on another, granting an allowance the signer never intended.
root_cause: Domain separator or nonce does not uniquely identify the chain/deployment (missing chainid, static DOMAIN_SEPARATOR, or reuse of the nonce after redeploy).
preconditions: permit-style signed approvals used
domain separator does not include chainid or a unique salt
signature can be observed on one chain and submitted on another
exploit_sequence: victim signs a permit on chain A
attacker replays the same signature on chain B where the contract shares the same address/domain
spender uses the replayed allowance to move the victim's funds on chain B
impact: Unauthorized transfer of funds via replayed signatures.
remediation: Include chainid in the EIP-712 domain, burn/replace nonces atomically on redeploy, and verify the recovered signer matches the expected owner.
code_evidence: bytes32 DOMAIN_SEPARATOR = keccak256(...); // static, no chainid
corrected_code: bytes32 DOMAIN_SEPARATOR = keccak256(abi.encode(TYPEHASH, name, version, block.chainid, address(this)));

source: standard ERC-20 behavior vs exploitable deviation (validator guidance)
mechanism: The approve/transferFrom allowance race (SWC-114) is standard ERC-20 semantics: a spender can spend the old allowance between the victim's approve() broadcast and its confirmation. Reporting it as a vulnerability is a false positive unless the code shows an exploitable deviation (e.g. approve to non-zero without zeroing, permit without reset).
root_cause: None — standard behavior; flagged as FP by deterministic rules when no deviation is shown.
preconditions: victim calls approve to change an allowance
spender has an existing nonzero allowance
no deviation such as missing zero-reset or permit without reset
exploit_sequence: victim broadcasts approve(newAmount)
spender front-runs: spends the old allowance in-flight
after approve confirms, spender spends the new allowance too
impact: Informational only — integrators should use increase/decreaseAllowance or zero-then-set. Not an exploitable deviation in the contract itself.
remediation: Use increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance, or approve(0) then approve(new) atomically; treat nonzero-over-nonzero approve as unsafe integration guidance.
code_evidence: function approve(address guy, uint wad) public returns (bool) { allowance[msg.sender][guy] = wad; return true; } // canonical
corrected_code: // integrator guidance only; the contract itself is standard ERC-20

mechanism: Contracts credit a user the requested deposit amount but receive less (fee-on-transfer/deflationary token), then allow withdrawal against the over-credited amount — the vault becomes insolvent.
root_cause: Bookkeeping uses the requested amount instead of the actual received balance delta.
preconditions: integrates arbitrary/defi token with transfer fees or deflation
credits the requested amount, not the measured received delta
withdrawals redeem against the inflated credit
exploit_sequence: deposit a fee-on-transfer token (contract credits full amount, receives less)
repeatedly deposit to build an inflated credit
withdraw the full credited amount, draining the underlying
remediation: Measure balance-before/balance-after per transfer and credit the delta; support only standard tokens or explicit fee-tolerant accounting.
code_evidence: IERC20(t).transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amt); shares += amt; // overcredits
corrected_code: uint before = t.balanceOf(address(this)); t.transferFrom(...); shares += t.balanceOf(address(this)) - before;

source: delegatecall to untrusted target / selfdestruct library (public corpus)
mechanism: A contract delegatecalls into a target that the caller can influence (untrusted library, unverified upgrade target, or a killable library), so arbitrary code runs in the caller's storage context — including selfdestruct of the caller or corruption of its state.
root_cause: Delegatecall target is not verified/immutable, or its address is caller-controlled; delegatecall inherits storage and msg.sender, so the callee can corrupt the caller.
preconditions: delegatecall/staticcall into a target whose code is not trusted
target address settable by a non-owner or an upgrade path without verification
or the target can selfdestruct, bricking all callers
exploit_sequence: attacker obtains control of the delegatecall target (init race, unguarded upgrade, library claim)
call the proxy/contract to trigger delegatecall
malicious target code selfdestructs the caller or rewrites its owner/admin storage
permanently brick or drain the contract
impact: Complete loss of funds or permanent bricking.
remediation: Delegatecall only into verified, immutable, audited logic; restrict target updates to a timelocked, verified admin path; never allow arbitrary addresses to become delegatecall targets.

source: token approval + burn order hazard (public audit corpus)
mechanism: An operation depends on an allowance being available at burn/transfer time, but a prior step (approve to zero, re-approve, or a fee deduction) removes the allowance first — causing the operation to revert or, in the unsafe direction, letting a stale allowance persist across an operation boundary.
root_cause: Allowance lifecycle not atomic with the operation that consumes it; state change order between approval and consumption is exploitable.
preconditions: a function approves then transfers/burns in sequence
another callable function can alter the allowance between the steps
or the allowance persists past the intended one-time use
exploit_sequence: attacker front-runs or interleaves an allowance mutation between approve and consume
consume fails (DoS) or a stale allowance remains for later abuse
repeat to grief or to spend beyond intent
remediation: Consume the allowance and perform the transfer in one atomic step; use safeIncrease/safeDecrease; zero out allowances after one-shot operations.
corrected_code: // pull the exact amount atomically; require(allowance >= amt); allowance -= amt; token.transferFrom(...);

mechanism: Governance executes a proposal in the same block it passes, and voting power can be flash-loaned, so an attacker can pass a malicious proposal and drain the treasury without holding long-term voting power.
root_cause: No delay between proposal approval and execution, combined with borrowable on-chain voting power.
preconditions: execution immediately follows passing (no timelock)
voting power snapshot is on-chain and borrowable via flash loan
the proposal can move funds or upgrade logic
exploit_sequence: flash-borrow governance tokens
pass a malicious proposal
execute it in the same transaction
steal funds and repay the flash loan
remediation: Enforce a timelock between vote and execution; make voting power non-flash-loanable (snapshot + delay); require a delay after large voting-power changes.
code_evidence: function execute(uint id) external { require(quorumMet(id)); _exec(id); } // same-block

source: read-only view consumed across contracts — access control (public corpus)
mechanism: A state-changing function lacks an authorization check and is externally reachable (no onlyOwner/onlyRole, no msg.sender validation), so any caller can invoke privileged behavior — mint, set owner, sweep, upgrade.
root_cause: Missing access modifier or caller validation on a privileged external function.
preconditions: function is external/public and state-changing
no onlyOwner/onlyRole modifier and no explicit msg.sender check
the function's effect is privileged (ownership change, mint, fund movement, upgrade)
exploit_sequence: attacker calls the unguarded function directly
gains ownership / mints / sweeps funds / upgrades logic
repeats as needed
impact: Full takeover or direct loss of funds.
remediation: Apply access modifiers to all privileged functions; add tests asserting non-privileged callers revert.
code_evidence: function setOwner(address o) external { owner = o; } // no check
corrected_code: function setOwner(address o) external onlyOwner { owner = o; }
